title: Rudin Ch 3: Numerical Sequences and Series

items.back: $p_{n}→p$ if for every $ε>0$ there is $N$ with $d(p_{n},p)<ε$ for all $n≥N$.
For $n_{1}<n_{2}<⋯$, $(p_{n_{i}})$ is a subsequence; its limit, if any, is a subsequential limit of $(p_{n})$.
For every $ε>0$ there is $N$ with $d(p_{n},p_{m})<ε$ for all $n,m≥N$.
$\mathrm{diam}\,E = \sup\{d(p,q): p,q∈E\}$.
Every Cauchy sequence converges. $ℝ^{k}$ and compact spaces are complete; $ℚ$ is not.
Increasing if $s_{n}≤s_{n+1}$ for all $n$; decreasing similarly.
For every $M$ there is $N$ with $s_{n}≥M$ for $n≥N$.
Let $E$ be the set of subsequential limits in the extended reals. $s^{*}=\sup E$, $s_{*}=\inf E$. Equivalently $\limsup s_{n} = \lim_{n}\sup_{k≥n}s_{k}$.
$Σa_{n}$ converges if the partial sums $s_{n}=a_{1}+⋯+a_{n}$ converge.
$Σc_{n}z^{n}$ with $R = 1/\limsup |c_{n}|^{1/n}$: converges absolutely for $|z|<R$, diverges for $|z|>R$.
$Σa_{n}$ converges absolutely if $Σ|a_{n}|$ converges.
$c_{n}=Σ_{k=0}^{n}a_{k}b_{n−k}$. A rearrangement is $Σa_{k_{n}}$ for a bijection $n↦k_{n}$ of $ℕ$.

In a metric space: $p_{n}→p$ iff every neighborhood of $p$ contains all but finitely many $p_{n}$; limits are unique; convergent sequences are bounded; if $p∈E'$ some sequence in $E$ converges to $p$.
Sums, scalar multiples, products and quotients (nonzero limit) of convergent complex sequences converge to the expected limits.
(a) Every sequence in a compact metric space has a convergent subsequence. (b) Every bounded sequence in $ℝ^{k}$ has a convergent subsequence.

items.front: Subsequential limits form a closed set
items.back: The set of subsequential limits of $(p_{n})$ is closed.
$\mathrm{diam}\,\bar E = \mathrm{diam}\,E$. If $K_{n}$ are nested nonempty compact sets with diameters $→0$, their intersection is exactly one point.
(a) Convergent ⇒ Cauchy in any metric space. (b) Cauchy ⇒ convergent in a compact space. (c) Cauchy ⇒ convergent in $ℝ^{k}$.
A monotone sequence converges iff it is bounded.
$s^{*}$ is itself a subsequential limit, and if $x>s^{*}$ then $s_{n}<x$ for all large $n$. It is the only number with both properties.
If $s_{n}≤t_{n}$ for $n≥N$, then $\liminf s_{n} ≤ \liminf t_{n}$ and $\limsup s_{n} ≤ \limsup t_{n}$.
$Σa_{n}$ converges iff for each $ε$ there's $N$ with $|Σ_{k=n}^{m}a_{k}|≤ε$ for $m≥n≥N$. Hence convergence forces $a_{n}→0$.
If $|a_{n}|≤c_{n}$ eventually and $Σc_{n}$ converges, so does $Σa_{n}$. If $a_{n}≥d_{n}≥0$ and $Σd_{n}$ diverges, so does $Σa_{n}$.
$Σx^{n}=1/(1−x)$ for $|x|<1$; diverges for $|x|≥1$.
If $a_{1}≥a_{2}≥⋯≥0$, then $Σa_{n}$ converges iff $Σ2^{k}a_{2^{k}}$ converges.
$Σ1/n^{p}$ converges iff $p>1$. $Σ1/(n(\log n)^{p})$ converges iff $p>1$.
$e = Σ1/n!$ $= \lim(1+1/n)^{n}$, and $e$ is irrational.
Root: $α=\limsup|a_{n}|^{1/n}$; converges if $α<1$, diverges if $α>1$. Ratio: converges if $\limsup|a_{n+1}/a_{n}|<1$; diverges if $|a_{n+1}/a_{n}|≥1$ eventually.
$\liminf\frac{c_{n+1}}{c_{n}} ≤ \liminf c_{n}^{1/n} ≤ \limsup c_{n}^{1/n} ≤ \limsup\frac{c_{n+1}}{c_{n}}$. The root test is stronger.
If partial sums of $Σa_{n}$ are bounded and $b_{n}$ decreases to 0, then $Σa_{n}b_{n}$ converges.
If $|c_{1}|≥|c_{2}|≥⋯$, $c_{n}→0$ and signs alternate, $Σc_{n}$ converges.
If $Σ|a_{n}|$ converges, so does $Σa_{n}$.
If $Σa_{n}$ converges absolutely to $A$ and $Σb_{n}$ converges to $B$, their Cauchy product converges to $AB$.
A conditionally convergent real series can be rearranged to converge to any value (or diverge). Absolutely convergent series: every rearrangement has the same sum.

items.modelProof: If $p_{n}→p$, pick $N$ with $d(p_{n},p)<ε/2$ for $n≥N$. Then $d(p_{n},p_{m}) ≤ d(p_{n},p)+d(p,p_{m})<ε$.

A Cauchy sequence is bounded (take $ε=1$). By Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a subsequence $p_{n_{i}}→p$. Given $ε$, choose $N$ from the Cauchy condition and $n_{i}≥N$ with $d(p_{n_{i}},p)<ε$; then $d(p_{n},p)<2ε$ for $n≥N$.
If $(s_{n})$ increases and is bounded, let $s=\sup s_{n}$. For $ε>0$, some $s_{N}>s−ε$, and then $s−ε<s_{N}≤s_{n}≤s$ for $n≥N$.

Group terms in blocks $[2^{k},2^{k+1})$. Since terms decrease, $s_{n} ≤ t_{k}=Σ_{j≤k}2^{j}a_{2^{j}}$ when $n<2^{k+1}$, and $s_{n} ≥ \tfrac12 t_{k}$ when $n>2^{k}$. So one sequence of partial sums is bounded iff the other is.
If $α<β<1$, then $|a_{n}|^{1/n}<β$ for large $n$ (3.17), so $|a_{n}|<β^{n}$ and compare with a geometric series. If $α>1$, then $|a_{n}|>1$ infinitely often, so $a_{n}\not→0$.
Let $s_{n}=Σ_{k≤n}1/k!$. Then $0<e−s_{n}<1/(n!\,n)$. If $e=m/n$, then $n!(e−s_{n})$ is a positive integer below $1/n≤1$, impossible.

items.prompt: Let $s_{1}=1$ and $s_{n+1}=\sqrt{3+2s_{n}}$. Prove $(s_{n})$ converges and find the limit.
items.modelProof: If $s_{n}<3$ then $s_{n+1}<\sqrt9=3$. And $s_{n+1}^{2}−s_{n}^{2}=3+2s_{n}−s_{n}^{2}=(3−s_{n})(1+s_{n})>0$. Monotone and bounded, so $s_{n}→L$ with $L=\sqrt{3+2L}$, i.e. $L^{2}−2L−3=0$, so $L=3$ (since $L≥1$).
The cosine takes values $\tfrac12,−\tfrac12,−1,−\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1$. Subsequential limits are $\{−1,−\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1\}$, so $\limsup=1$ and $\liminf=−1$.

items.hint: Ratio test; telescoping; rationalize; limit comparison with $1/n$.
items.modelProof: (a) Ratio $=(n/(n+1))^{n}→1/e<1$: converges. (b) Partial sums $\sqrt{N+1}−1→∞$: diverges. (c) Term $=1/(n(\sqrt{n+1}+\sqrt n))≤1/(2n^{3/2})$: converges. (d) $n^{1/n}→1$, so term$/(1/n)→1$: diverges.

items.prompt: Find the radius of convergence of (a) $Σ(n!/n^{n})z^{n}$ (b) $Σ z^{n^{2}}/2^{n}$.
items.hint: Use 3.37 for (a); for (b) the nonzero coefficients sit at $k=n^{2}$.
items.modelProof: (a) Ratio of coefficients $→1/e$, so $R=e$. (b) $c_{k}=2^{−n}$ when $k=n^{2}$, else 0. $|c_{k}|^{1/k}=2^{−1/n}→1$ along those $k$, so $\limsup=1$ and $R=1$.
$\sqrt{a_{n}}/n ≤ \tfrac12(a_{n}+1/n^{2})$, and both series on the right converge.

items.prompt: If $a_{n}>0$ and $a_{n+1}/a_{n}<1$ for every $n$, then $Σa_{n}$ converges.
items.explanation: $a_{n}=1/n$. The ratio must stay below some fixed $β<1$, not just below 1.

items.prompt: If every subsequence of $(s_{n})$ has a further subsequence converging to $s$, then $s_{n}→s$.
items.explanation: Otherwise some $ε$ and some subsequence stay at distance $≥ε$ from $s$; none of its sub-subsequences can converge to $s$.

items.prompt: $\limsup(s_{n}+t_{n}) ≤ \limsup s_{n} + \limsup t_{n}$ (when the right side is not $∞−∞$).
A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.
items.explanation: Same argument as 3.11(c), in any metric space.

items.claim: Every Cauchy sequence in a metric space converges.
lines: By Bolzano–Weierstrass it has a convergent subsequence, and a Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges.
items.explanation: Bolzano–Weierstrass holds in $ℝ^{k}$ (and in compact spaces), not in every metric space. In $ℚ$, truncations of $\sqrt2$ are Cauchy with no limit.
You can't send the base to its limit while leaving the exponent $n$ free; both depend on $n$. The actual limit is $e$ (3.31).

lines: By the Cauchy criterion we need $|a_{n+1}+⋯+a_{m}|$ small.
Each $|a_{k}|<ε$ for large $k$, so the sum is small.
items.explanation: The block has $m−n$ terms, which can be huge, so the bound is $(m−n)ε$, not $ε$. Harmonic series is the counterexample.

items.name: Harmonic series $Σ1/n$
items.details: Terms $→0$ yet the series diverges. Also shows $s_{n+1}−s_{n}→0$ does not imply Cauchy.

items.name: $Σ(−1)^{n+1}/n$
items.details: Converges (to $\log 2$) but not absolutely; rearrangements can change its sum (3.54).

items.name: $Σ1/n$ vs $Σ1/n^{2}$
items.details: Ratio and root tests both give limit 1 for each, yet one diverges and one converges.

items.name: Decimal truncations of $\sqrt2$ in $ℚ$
items.details: Cauchy in $ℚ$ with no limit in $ℚ$, so $ℚ$ is not complete.

items.name: An enumeration of $ℚ∩[0,1]$
items.details: Every point of $[0,1]$ is a subsequential limit (consistent with 3.7: the set is closed).
